title: What are bonds? How they work and how to invest in India
summary: What a bond is, how coupon, yield and price work, why prices fall when rates rise, the main types, the risks and how to buy in India.
body_markdown:
A bond is a loan you make to a government or a company. In return it pays you interest, usually at a fixed rate, and repays your money on a set date. Its price can move before then, mostly with interest rates. The borrower is called the issuer.


Picture a first-time saver with ₹10,000, choosing between a bond and a fixed deposit. The differences sit in who you lend to, how you can get out early, and what protects you if things go wrong.


## What is a bond?


A bond is a loan you make to an issuer, which pays you interest and returns your money on a set date. Issuers in India fall into a few groups.


- **The Central Government** issues government securities, called G-secs, and treasury bills.
- **State governments** issue state development loans, or SDLs.
- **PSUs** are public sector undertakings: companies that the central or a state government controls, usually by owning at least 51%.
- **Companies** issue bonds. A non-convertible debenture, or NCD, is a bond a company issues that cannot be turned into shares.
- **Civic bodies** , such as city corporations, issue municipal bonds.


## How does a bond pay you?


Most bonds pay a fixed amount of interest, the coupon, at set intervals, and repay the face value at maturity. Face value is the amount the issuer repays at maturity, and the coupon is paid on it. Maturity is the date the issuer repays it. The coupon is a percentage of face value.


Take a bond with a face value of ₹10,000 and a 7.5% coupon. It pays ₹750 a year and returns ₹10,000 at maturity. Real government bonds pay twice a year; this example uses one yearly payment to keep the sums simple.


- Dated G-secs carry a fixed or floating coupon, paid every six months. They generally run from 5 years to 40 years.
- SDLs pay interest every six months and repay the principal on the maturity date.
- Treasury bills pay no interest. They are sold at a discount and repaid at face value. The[treasury bills guide](https://koshex.com/blog/treasury-bills) covers them.
- A floating-rate bond's interest is not fixed. It is reset at set intervals, say every six months, in line with a benchmark rate.


## Coupon, current yield and yield to maturity: what is the difference?


The coupon is the interest on face value. The current yield is that interest divided by today's price. The yield to maturity (YTM) is your whole return if you hold to maturity at today's price.


Say similar bonds now yield 8.5%, so the ₹10,000 bond above trades at about ₹9,672 with four years left. A buyer at that price gets:


Measure Working Result


Coupon rate ₹750 on a face value of ₹10,000 7.5%, unchanged


Current yield ₹750 ÷ ₹9,672 7.75%


Yield to maturity ₹750 a year, plus ₹10,000 back for ₹9,672 8.5%


The YTM is higher than the coupon because ₹10,000 comes back for ₹9,672. This is an illustration on a hypothetical bond, not a forecast.


## Why do bond prices fall when interest rates rise?


When new bonds pay more, an older bond with a lower coupon is worth less, so its price drops until its yield matches the new level. The RBI puts it plainly: if market interest rates rise, the price of a bond falls.


For the same bond:


Yield on similar bonds Price of this bond


8.5% about ₹9,672


7.5% ₹10,000


6.5% about ₹10,343


Price here is the present value of the bond's remaining payments, as the RBI defines it. When you read that G-sec yields are rising, G-sec prices are falling.


Per AMFI, how far the price moves depends on the bond's coupon and maturity. The RBI says small investors can reduce market risk by holding to maturity, which lets them realise the yield at which they bought. Buy at ₹10,000 and hold, and the promised payments are still ₹750 a year and ₹10,000 at the end, unless the issuer fails to pay. Sell early, and SEBI's investor website warns that you can make a loss.


[How interest rates affect mutual funds](https://koshex.com/blog/how-interest-rates-affect-mutual-funds) explains the same effect for funds that hold bonds.


## What types of bonds are there in India?


Bonds are sorted by who issues them and by how they pay.


Type Issuer How it pays


Dated government securities Central Government Fixed or floating coupon, every six months


State development loans State governments Interest every six months


[Treasury bills](https://koshex.com/blog/treasury-bills) Central Government No coupon; sold at a discount, repaid at face value


[PSU and corporate bonds, NCDs](https://koshex.com/blog/corporate-bonds-and-ncds) PSUs and companies As each bond's terms say


[Tax-free bonds](https://koshex.com/blog/what-is-tax-free-bonds-features-benefits) Public-sector companies, in past years Interest exempt from income tax under Schedule II of the Income-tax Act, 2025


Floating-rate bonds Government Coupon reset at set intervals


Zero-coupon bonds and STRIPS Government, and some companies and banks Issued at a discount, redeemed at face value. The Government has not issued zero-coupon bonds since 1996


Capital and inflation indexed bonds Government Principal linked to an inflation index; inflation indexed bonds also protect the coupon


Municipal bonds Civic bodies As each bond's terms say; a credit rating is required


Sovereign gold bonds RBI, for the Government 2.50% a year on the initial investment, half-yearly, on a bond denominated in grams of gold; eight years. The last issue was in February 2024


RBI Floating Rate Savings Bonds Central Government For residents, not NRIs; seven years; NSC rate plus 0.35 percentage point, reset every six months; not tradable; taxable


STRIPS are created by separating the cash flows of a G-sec. Sovereign gold bonds already issued can be bought and sold on the stock exchange and on the RBI's platform.


## Are bonds safe?


A bond is only as safe as its issuer's ability to pay and the price you can sell at. Default means the borrower fails to pay on time. The RBI says government securities carry practically no risk of default. That statement is about government securities only. AMFI adds that corporate bonds carry a higher amount of credit risk.


A credit rating is the rating agency's opinion of how likely a debt is to be repaid in full and on time. SEBI's scale for long-term securities runs from AAA, the highest degree of safety and lowest credit risk, through AA (high safety) and A (adequate safety) to BBB (moderate). BB, B and C signal moderate, high and very high risk of default. D means in default, or expected to be soon.


Grades from AA to C can carry a + or -. BBB- is the lowest investment-grade rating. A rating is an opinion, not a promise. It is not a recommendation to buy, hold or sell, and it can change quickly. The[corporate bonds guide](https://koshex.com/blog/corporate-bonds-and-ncds) goes deeper on ratings and defaults.


The RBI names other risks even for government bonds: market risk (prices move against you when rates change) and liquidity risk (no quick buyer at a fair price).


Deposit insurance, DICGC cover of up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, applies to bank deposits only. It does not cover company deposits or bonds.


## How can you buy bonds in India?


You can buy bonds in India through RBI Retail Direct for government bonds, through a broker on the stock exchange for listed bonds, in a public NCD issue, or on a SEBI-registered online bond platform. A demat account, with a SEBI-registered depository participant, holds your securities in electronic form. You buy and sell them on a stock exchange through a trading account with a SEBI-registered stockbroker.


Route What you can buy What you need


RBI Retail Direct Central and state government bonds, treasury bills, sovereign gold bonds PAN, rupee savings account, KYC document, email, mobile


Stock exchange, via a broker Listed bonds A demat account and a trading account


Public NCD issue NCDs a company offers to the public ASBA, where your bank blocks the application money in your account, or a UPI block for applications up to ₹5 lakh


SEBI-registered online bond platform Listed debt, public-issue debt, listed G-secs, SDLs, treasury bills, listed sovereign gold bonds A platform registered with SEBI as a stock broker


Privately placed bonds usually trade in lots of ₹10,000 or ₹1 lakh, because SEBI sets their face value and the trading lot equals it. A public NCD issue stays open for two to ten working days and lists within three working days after. A registered platform may not offer unlisted bonds. SEBI's press release of 19 November 2025 urges investors to avoid unregistered online bond platforms and to verify registration. The[corporate bonds guide](https://koshex.com/blog/corporate-bonds-and-ncds) has the detail.


### How can you buy government bonds directly from the RBI?


RBI Retail Direct lets you open a free government securities account with the RBI using your PAN and Indian bank account, and bid from ₹10,000 in auctions of central and state government bonds and T-bills. RBI calls it a Retail Direct Gilt (RDG) account. Government securities are also called gilt-edged instruments. Eligible NRIs can open one too. The[treasury bills guide](https://koshex.com/blog/treasury-bills) covers the account and bidding in detail.


## Bonds, FDs or a debt fund: what is the difference?


A bond is a loan to one issuer that you hold yourself. An FD is a deposit with a bank or company. A debt fund spreads your money across many bonds and has no fixed return. A debt fund is a mutual fund that buys bonds.


**Spreading the risk.** A single bond rides on one issuer. SEBI limits how much of a debt fund can sit with one borrower. The cap is 10% of the fund if the borrower's paper is rated AAA, 8% if AA and 6% if A or lower. This applies to actively managed schemes other than credit risk funds. Mutual funds may hold only investment-grade securities.


**Getting out early.** An individual's bank FD of up to ₹1 crore can be closed early; the bank pays the rate for the time it ran, minus any penalty it has disclosed. A bond needs a buyer at the market price, so, like the ₹10,000 bond above, it can sell for less than its face value. A debt fund can be redeemed at its NAV, the price of one unit.


**What you earn.** An FD's rate is fixed for its term. The interest from a debt fund's bonds goes to the fund and lifts its value each day. It reaches you as a higher NAV, or as an IDCW payout if you picked that option. No mutual fund pays a fixed interest rate.


**Tax.** Interest on bonds, debentures, NCDs and government securities is taxed under income from other sources at your slab rate, as FD interest is. A Specified Mutual Fund is one with more than 65% of its money in debt and money market instruments. Gains on its units bought on or after 1 April 2023 are taxed at slab rates, whatever the holding period. TDS, tax deducted before money reaches you, is not cut on central or state government bonds and treasury bills, except named taxable savings bonds such as the Floating Rate Savings Bonds 2020. For a resident, listed corporate bonds carry 10% TDS on the whole year's interest from one issuer once it passes ₹10,000. The[bond tax guide](https://koshex.com/blog/taxation-of-bond-investments) covers gains.


See[debt mutual funds vs fixed deposits](https://koshex.com/blog/debt-mutual-funds-vs-fixed-deposits) for that comparison, and the pages on[debt funds](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories/debt-funds) ,[gilt funds](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories/gilt-funds) ,[corporate bond funds](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories/corporate-bond-funds) and[target maturity funds](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories/target-maturity-funds) .
